text: It's MORNING EDITION from NPR News. Good morning. I'm Steve Inskeep.

And I'm Renee Montagne. An unusual battle is brewing here in California, pitting solar energy against trees. It began when one home owner with solar panels revived an obscure environmental state law that's bad news for his neighbor's redwood trees.
David Gorn reports from Silicon Valley on the struggle over the right to sunlight.

Richard Treanor recycles, and his neighbor Mark Vargus, he recycles, too. Treanor has energy saving appliances and neighbor Vargus has energy saving appliances, too. They both have electric cars. In terms of loving the environment it seems neither one can top the other. But Treanor discovered he was on the losing end of environmentalism when he found himself being tried in state court for planting eight redwood trees.
We're not criminals. My wife and I do not consider ourselves criminals. And yet we found ourselves in Superior Court, right next to the guys with the orange jumpsuits and shackles.

The problem is Treanor's trees are casting a large shadow on his next door neighbor and that neighbor's array of solar panels. In what seems to be the first ruling of its kind in the nation, a Superior Court judge ordered Treanor to cut down two of his eight trees. That's because of a unique and little used law, the California Solar Shade Control Act. It was passed back in 1979, after the oil crisis and lines at the gas station convinced lawmakers of the importance of alternative energy. Solar power, the law basically says, is more important than any trees that shade them. To Treanor that message makes no sense.
We want to put solar on all - everybody's roofs and everything and whack the trees down? I don't think so.

But to neighbor Mark Vargus it's not so simple. When those redwood saplings were planted behind his fence line ten years ago they were about five feet tall. Now, they're topping 35 feet. And they could eventually loom 100 feet or more over his small and now very dark backyard. And that's the problem.
Here you see 40 modules on the west side, which produce the greatest amount of power somewhere in the neighborhood of probably 2:00 to 4:00, somewhere in that range.

Vargus is walking around his home, pointing out the solar panels covering much of his roof. Most them are so high up they're currently unaffected by the redwoods, but a set of solar panels in the backyard can't get any sun to generate power. Even though he installed his solar panels after the trees were planted, Vargus still feels he's entitled to the sunlight that's supposed to fall in his backyard. And the law says his solar panels demand it.

The law protects solar power. Thirty years ago, I don't think it was as important as it is now. Without the rights of solar access, maybe more people would not even consider putting solar in if they weren't protected.

The whole dispute, says Ken Rosenblatt of the Santa Clara county district attorney's office, has put him and every D.A. in the state in a bad spot. That's because the law requires him to treat shade producing trees as a public nuisance hazard, just like piles of trash or toxic waste.

I would much rather be pursuing polluters than trying to cut down trees, but our duty is to enforce the law and the legislature has made it clear that my duty is also to protect the solar collectors from the trees that are casting shade on it.

Now, Treanor says this battle isn't really over solar power, that his neighbor is just using this old law to get rid of trees he doesn't like. And Vargus says this is the ultimate case of not in my backyard, because his neighbors say they're pro-solar but are fighting the law anyway.

So yes, this is about solar panels versus trees, but it also has a more familiar ring to it. At its root, this back and forth neighbor dispute is really like thousands of property line feuds throughout California and the nation. And that's the real danger, says Frank Schiavo, longtime environmental studies teacher at San Jose State University.
In practical terms, I think it's going to open a floodgate, so to speak, of conflicts between neighbors.

Schiavo says that Vargus may be the first to use the Solar Shade Act, but now that's it's succeeded, he won't be the last. Treanor is appealing the judge's ruling, but also says he's set to cut down two of his eight trees to end the whole thing. Vargus says the ruling simply upholds the law and he may go after two more of the trees next year.
For NPR News, I'm David Gorn.
This is DAY TO DAY. I'm Alex Chadwick.

I'm Madeleine Brand. The big cats are back at the San Francisco Zoo. Two months after a teenager was killed by a Siberian tiger, the remaining zoo cats are finally back on public display today. They're in an outdoor enclosure with much higher walls, protective glass, and 8,000-volt electrified wires. David Gorn reports from San Francisco.

The tiger and lion exhibits at the San Francisco Zoo have been closed off since Christmas Day. That's when one tiger escaped its enclosure, attacked three zoo patrons and mauled one of them to death. The escaped tiger was killed.
Since then, all the other big cats at the zoo have had to stay inside while construction workers built up their outdoor enclosures.

speaker_label: Mr. BOB JENKINS (Director of Animal Care, San Francisco Zoo)
text: Well, right now we're standing in front of one of the tiger grottos here at the Lion House at the San Francisco Zoo.

Bob Jenkins is director of animal care at San Francisco Zoo. The walls around the big cats are now taller, he says, four feet taller. On top of that are five-foot-high glass panels set in steel supports, and along the sides of the inner wall are electrified wires with 8,000 volts running through them. This is about as safe as you can get, Jenkins says.
That's George. He's a 300-pound Sumatran tiger, and he's roaming back and forth in his new digs, testing it out.
The tiger is talking, Jenkins says, to his female mate one enclosure over.

speaker_label: Mr. BOB JENKINS (Director of Animal Care, San Francisco Zoo)
text: He's calling, she's replying, and you can liken it to, I guess, sending love notes to each other.

The tiger incident happened at closing time, Jenkins says, when only about 20 people were sprinkled throughout the park. People have speculated that the tiger was taunted and goaded into retaliation, but no one actually saw the incident. So nobody knows exactly what happened, Jenkins says, except the three victims and the two Siberian tigers in the enclosure.

speaker_label: Mr. BOB JENKINS (Director of Animal Care, San Francisco Zoo)
text: It's quite clear, at least to me, that there was something significant that night. I don't know what it was, but something significant happened.
So since then the animals have been kept indoors on a time-out for 52 days.

speaker_label: Ms. BARBARA PALMER (Chief Feline Keeper, San Francisco Zoo)
text: Come on, babe.
Barbara Palmer has been the primary keeper of the lions and tigers over those long two months.

speaker_label: Ms. BARBARA PALMER (Chief Feline Keeper, San Francisco Zoo)
text: I think we saw a little bit of what I describe as cabin fever, just a little bit of crabbiness sometimes.
She says the trick was to constantly keep the giant felines busy.

speaker_label: Ms. BARBARA PALMER (Chief Feline Keeper, San Francisco Zoo)
text: Cat toys, bones to chew on, blood popsicles is a favorite.

And animal handlers kept the tigers' and lions' attention diverted with a TV set. They saw videos of the African plains set to Beethoven music - and, yes, it's true: a particular favorite of one tiger was the Disney cartoon "The Lion King."
(As Pumbaa the Warthog) Hey kid, what's eatin' ya?
(As Young Simba) I don't want to talk about it.
(As Timon the Meerkat) He looks blue.
(As Pumbaa) I'd say brownish-gold.

So finally a few days ago the big cats got to stretch their legs in the new enclosures, and even though the public was not allowed to walk by the pens, that didn't stop half-a-dozen zoo-goers, including Cathy Carsky(ph) of Elmira, New York, who peered through a Plexiglas window at the far end of the lions den.
We were wondering if over there, where the wire is, and then you could see the electrical, is that where he got out?

Carsky says that she was standing at this lion window earlier, when a family came up to it and starting pounding on the window - the kids, the parents, all of them - to try to get the lions to do something. As Carsky put it, some people just don't learn.
For NPR News, I'm David Gorn in San Francisco.
Now, what happens to an endangered species when it makes a spectacular comeback? That's the topic of this week's Science Out of the Box.

Take elephant seals. Every year on beach in central California is overrun by thousands of these giant animals. The mating season is now winding down. This year it set a new record for the number of elephant seals hitting the beach and the number of baby seals born. There were so many crowding the beaches near San Simeon that they started to venture toward the nearby highway, and that wasn't good for man or car or beast.
David Gorn reports.

There's an amazing sight along the remote stretch of beach north of San Luis Obispo. About 6,000 to 8,000 northern elephant seals jammed onto a narrow strip of sand. These are huge animals - some of the 16 feet long and 5,000 pounds of blubber and muscle. There isn't an inch between them, and the pack of them stretches on and on along the beach. And these are loud animals.

Now, that's not flatulence and belching, that's lovemaking. These elephant seals have migrated all the way from the Gulf of Alaska. They come to this spot every winter to breed - and to fight off other elephant seals - and then, says long-time elephant seal observer, Lou Tornadski(ph), to breed some more.
And it's a sort of all basic. So, you have all the ingredients. There's conflict, there's lust, there's birthing. It's kind of like a Mel Gibson movie without the bad dialogue.
In fact, this chaos is like the elephant seal version of spring break. And just like unruly college kids, these wild animals can get into trouble.
Sometimes these elephant seals try to run across the road. Only this road is Highway 1.
You know, it's a real hazard to both wildlife and the people driving.

That's marine biologist Brian Hatfield. He says that even though there have only been a handful of car collisions with elephant seals over the years, the problem is becoming much bigger now. There are so many more seals now, and the fences containing them have begun to fall apart. Hatfield found himself trying to herd a 1,500-pound seal back across the road. And he found out that you can't really tell an elephant seal where to go.
If you get them to move in the direction you want it to but then it seems like they make up their own mind.
It took the combined forces of State Parks, Fish and Game, the Marine Mammal Center, and the Highway Patrol to stop traffic for a few hours one morning and shoo the reluctant beast back to the beach.

But other incidents have been less controlled. There was the famous night when a family of tourists had their Nissan Pathfinder pulverized. And when the passenger in the car saw this 10-foot-high one-ton pile of blubber with large teeth rearing up in the high beams, she thought it was a monster.
I can believe that in the dark. And if you're not somebody who's very familiar with the seals it would look like a monster.

Biologist Patricia Morris works with elephant seals farther north near Santa Cruz. She says that usually elephant seals end up on extremely remote beaches. The San Simeon beaches are the only elephant seal breeding grounds right up against the highway.

But it's not just the highway and the occasional one-ton road kill that Morris is worried about. With so many elephant seals in close proximity to so many people, it's only a matter of time, she says, before something bad happens.
Sooner or later somebody's going to be killed directly by an elephant seal. It will happen some day. You know, there are always people who got to go press their luck.
Because resting elephant seals can look so calm and placid lying in the sand, people get really close to them, Morris says. People forget they're dealing with wild animals. Very large wild animals.

Cal Transit's working on making it safer by reinforcing the fences to keep elephant seals away from the highway. And, of course, new fences are eventually going to have to be built because as the elephant seal population continues to expand, those seals are moving farther and farther down the coast.
For NPR News, I'm David Gorn.
This is Day to Day. I'm Alex Chadwick.
And I'm Madeleine Brand.
In a few minutes, more than 50 African-Americans convert to Judaism in a small, southern Illinois town.

First, aid to China to help recover from the devastating earthquake. A Russian plane arrived today with 30 tons of food and blankets for Sichuan's provincial capital, Chengdu. This is the first international aid to reach the region.
Japan has pledged nearly five million dollars in cash and supplies, and France says it is sending a cargo plane loaded with tents, sleeping bags, tarps, and cooking kits.

The earthquake is spurring private relief efforts here, in the U.S. as well. Nearly one fifth of San Francisco is Chinese-American, and for many, the distant disaster feels very close. From member station KQED, David Gorn, reports.
On the top floor of China Town's Baptist Church about 30 recent immigrants are taking a literacy class.   ..TEXT: (Soundbite of people speaking Chinese)

Teacher Mimi Wong(ph) is talking about the subject on everyone's mind, the 7.9 earthquake that shook central China Monday. She has an envelope at the front of the class for people to make donations for earthquake relief. Even though these immigrants don't have much money, they slip a check into the envelope on their way into, or out of class. Wong tears up as she asks her students when they first heard about the earthquake?
(Through Translator) We are just kind of sad. That's way I'm a little emotional. He just said that is so sad inside, that we are just numb with grief.

None of the students in this adult literacy class is from the quake region. Like most of the Chinese-American population in this area, they come from southern China. They may not have friends, or family members affected by the quake, but says Wong, they all still the full weight of the disaster.
(Through translator) Because we are Chinese, we are bonded together.

Later Wong says she'll walk that envelope, stuffed with donations, down to the local Chinese newspaper, Sing Tao. The advertising office there is collecting money to give to the Red Cross.  The paper ran a full page ad asking for donations. Editor Tim Lau says the response, so far, has been overwhelming.
When the readers read about the ad, they go straight to our local office in San Francisco's China Town and there's a line out there. People are lining up to donate money to the earthquake victims.

At the head of that line to donate is Marina Lu(ph).  She says that everyone in her family, her father, her brother, her sister, they all plan to give. In fact, when the newspaper tries to take her picture because she's the first one to donate, she says no, she doesn't want any kind of special recognition.

Everybody is very shocked, you know, even though we are not living over there right, but we are Chinese. We feel the shock, like everybody around the world. You know, everybody should be doing something.

Across the Bay Bridge to Oakland. This working class city has a partnership with earthquake ravaged Mianyang, China.  They are friendship cities, similar to sister cities. Oakland City Councilman, Henry Chang was born in China, and says he's visited Mianyang about a dozen times in the last decade. So far, he hasn't been able to reach anyone he knows there.
There is over 7,000 people that die from that, and also at least, another 18,000 is right now still bury.

Chang is offered to send a search and rescue team from Oakland to Mianyang. It's the same crew, he says, that went to New York City after 9/11. And he says it's one of the few teams in the country that specialize in finding, and pulling people, from collapsed buildings. Chang worries when they arrive in China, it may be even more chaotic than September 11th.
When I heard 7.9, knowing the type of structure over there, in China mostly like bricks and other reinforced type of structure, so I know that it is going to be really tough.

Chang learned from his many trips to Mianyang that it's a poor city, and will take years to rebuild. The Chinese American community here in the Bay area, has been willing to step up in the past, after the Indian Ocean Tsunami, the Sin Tao newspaper group raised more than a million dollars. This time they expect donations will far exceed that total.
For NPR News, I'm David Gorn in San Francisco.
You know, listeners can't really see you, Alex, as being radio, but a few hours ago, you were pretty sweaty.
I prefer to think of it as a healthy glow. One of the side benefits of my commute to work today by bicycle. This is Ride Your Bike to Work week and we'll have more on that coming up.
There's more in a moment on Day to Day.
This is Day to Day. I'm Alex Cohen.

I'm Madeleine Brand. Firefighters in California continue to battle more than 1,000 firefighters - wildfires - I'll get that out. Now, they got some bad news yesterday. In scenic Big Sur, the fire there jumped the fire line and everyone was told to evacuate there. The fires have stretched California's firefighting resources, and so homeowners and business are now turning to private firms to protect their investments. David Gorn reports.
In the town of Ukiah, the timber town in the north part of California, fires dot the landscape. And part of that landscape belongs to Mike Jani, president of the Mendocino Redwood Company.
Jani's tiny office is now command central for helping coordinate firefighting efforts across 225,000 acres of his company's timber forest.
The afternoons get really busy as the fog pulls back and the wind picks up.
Jani has one wall buried in a dozen or more thick maps where you can see all the fires on his property at a glance.
This is - using Google Earth, we can get the lightning strikes, infrared strikes. Then we overlay it across our property so that you can see how many places we had lightning strikes.

Ninety-one lightning strikes, to be exact, on this property alone. And that sparked 31 fast-moving wildfires. CalFire crews can't possibly get to all the fires here. Jani felt he couldn't just sit back and watch parts of the forest burn. So he hired more than 100 private firefighters who came in from Montana, Idaho and Oregon. Jani even rented a helicopter with one of those big waterbag devices hanging from it.
They were flying from the ocean and dipping in the ocean and taking bucket after bucket after bucket and hitting hot spots, as the fire flared up, to keep it contained.

It was a first for Jani, though he says other timber companies in the nation have done the same thing. But most private homeowners probably can't afford a helicopter, much less a private firefighting crew. That's were Matt Bettencourt(ph) and AIG Insurance Company come in.
And that's all your property? Is your property line pretty obvious?
It goes to the middle of the creek.
Middle of the creek? And how about up top to the road?
Pretty much fenced.
OK.
So everyone will have to...

Bettencourt works for Firebreak Spray Systems, a company that's implementing a new and unique wildlife protection plan in partnership with AIG. He's visiting an AIG insured home in Orinda, one of the affluent zip codes in the San Francisco Bay Area, to evaluate fire danger and possibly spray a fire retardant on the property. Homeowner Karen Rhode (ph) says the smell of smoke in the air is what prompted her to call.
I'll tell you, lately that smoggy, gross - because it's really been, ew. It just makes you - it heightens your awareness to say, oh my gosh, I do live in an area that is susceptible to fires.

And there are many more of those susceptible areas, as bigger, expensive homes are built in more remote areas, the so-called urban-wildlife interface. AIG Insurance has actually created a wildfire division within its home insurance company. And an AIG spokesman says enrollment in the high end program has doubled since the start of the year. To Caroll Wills of the California Professional Firefighters Union, that's all fine. Good to have a number of companies pitch in and help. Good to have insurance companies act and to have homes fire protected. As long as all of this doesn't get out of hand, he says.
It's simply not practical or desirable or, in our view, safe, to have armies of individual fire departments combing the urban wildlife interface, especially when these cataclysms erupt.
And it could turn into a logistical nightmare, says Bill Stewart, UC Berkeley professor of forest economics.

Say you're going to have - you know, the companies will have these maps of, you know, which house you're responsible for or which ones you're not. So you're going to have, basically, private fire districts, local fire districts, state fire districts and the Feds. And you can imagine lots of time spent trying to figure out who's doing what.

California's struggle with so many fires and limited resources is liable to intensify, Stewart says, as the fire season wears on. And one way or another, he says, there is likely to be more and more private money involved to pay for it. For NPR News, I'm David Gorn.

To another hi-tech triumph now, bullet trains. Across the globe, high-speed rail systems have been a hit, whisking people around Europe and Asia. But not in the U.S., not yet. That could change if voters in California endorse a $10 billion ballot measure to create high-speed that would zip along at 220 miles an hour. David Gorn has the story.
When most people think of trains, it's the old reliable commuter cars.

Rattling passed towns, shaking the street as they rumble by. That is not what California has in mind. The proposed high-speed rail system in proposition 1-A would be whisper-quiet, running on electricity, not diesel. And the trains would be so fast, you could travel from San Francisco to Los Angeles in about two and a half hours. The revolutionary rail project would cost $45 billion and link all the major cities in the state.  And to Quentin Kopp, chair of the California High-Speed Authority, the cost is well worth the future benefit.

speaker_label: Mr. QUENTIN KOPP (Chair, California High-Speed Authority)
text: It's the largest project in terms of cost in the history of California, but so was the Transcontinental Railroad in terms of the United States of America. But look what the Transcontinental Railroad did for the United States of America and then start thinking about what high-speed rail is going to do for the state of California.    ..TEXT: GORN: At the main San Francisco train station, where it currently runs commuter rail down to San Jose, crowds are boiling out of the morning trains.

speaker_label: Mr. QUENTIN KOPP (Chair, California High-Speed Authority)
text: Unidentified Man #1: All aboard.

speaker_label: Mr. QUENTIN KOPP (Chair, California High-Speed Authority)
text: Unidentified Man #2: Yeah, Let's go. No, no, no. Where are you going?

speaker_label: Mr. QUENTIN KOPP (Chair, California High-Speed Authority)
text: Unidentified Man #3: San Jose.

speaker_label: Mr. QUENTIN KOPP (Chair, California High-Speed Authority)
text: Unidentified Man #2: Yeah, just get on.
Among the crowd is Assemblywoman Fiona Ma. She says, now may finally be the right time for California to move on this massive mass transit project.

speaker_label: Assemblywoman FIONA MA (Democratic, San Francisco, California)
text: This is the perfect storm here. The high cost of gasoline is keeping people out of their cars, the amount of hassle you face when you go to the airports, and just our whole awareness on global warming.

Supporters say that the high-speed rail systems in other countries all generate revenue. They are fast and efficient, and they keep cars off the roads. So, if high-speed rail is so terrific, and it's needed so badly, why hasn't it caught on in this country? Well, there is the overall $45 billion price tag for one thing, for which the $10 billion bond measure would be a sort of down payment.

That high price has prompted the California Chamber of Commerce to come out against it. And Jon Coupal of the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers' Association says the actual cost could be much higher than estimates. At a time when state and national budgets are so tight, he says, we could use that money for many other things. For example, Coupla says...

speaker_label: Mr. JON COUPAL (President, Howard Jarvis Taxpayer's Association)
text: Do we need high-speed rail more than we need surface water storage? Before we take on a high-tech transportation system that's unproven for this state, why don't we take care of something we know we actually need?
One other opposition voice when states have tried to create high-speed rail has been the airline industry. Quentin Kopp of the rail authority.

speaker_label: Mr. QUENTIN KOPP (Chair, California High-Speed Authority)
text: In Texas, Southwest Airlines quelled it because they didn't want competition.
Southwest did file a lawsuit opposing the Texas project. But so far, in California, the airlines have been quiet about the measure. And Kopp says he knows why.

speaker_label: Mr. QUENTIN KOPP (Chair, California High-Speed Authority)
text: Because the short haul don't make money for airlines. And by that, I mean trips of 300, 400 miles. And high-speed rail is perfect for that.
If California passes its bond measure in November, then it will be the first in the nation to launch high-speed rail. But Kopp says, it wouldn't be the last.

speaker_label: Mr. QUENTIN KOPP (Chair, California High-Speed Authority)
text: States all over the country are planning high-speed rail. Ohio is planning it, Illinois, Missouri. The Northwest is planning it.
And all keep an eye on California. Right now, polls say that most people don't know much about the proposition. But of those who do, a majority of voters favor it. For NPR News, I'm David Gorn.
